title: Why lives differ
hook: why some are short-lived, some sickly, some wise: deeds

segments.voice: Yesterday: atappa, explained by three monks, and your line, today, the effort. Did you give ten honest minutes to the thing you'd put off? Today, an old question. Day five hundred one.

Two kids are born in the same hospital on the same night. One grows up healthy and comfortable; the other struggles with illness and money for years. Why the difference? A young brahmin named Subha, Todeyya's son, put that question to the Buddha. You met Subha a few weeks ago, asking about the way to Brahma. Here, in the hundred and thirty-fifth discourse, he lays out seven pairs. Why are some people short-lived and some long-lived? Sickly and healthy? Plain and beautiful? Powerless and influential? Poor and rich? Low-born and high-born? Foolish and wise? Today: why lives differ.
screen: `SAME HOSPITAL, SAME NIGHT.` → `SUBHA, TODEYYA'S SON.` → `SEVEN PAIRS OF LIVES.`

segments.voice: The Buddha first answers in one dense line, paraphrased here: beings are owners of their deeds, heirs of their deeds. They're born of their deeds, bound to their deeds, and have their deeds as their refuge. It's deeds, kamma, that sort beings into lower and higher. Subha says: I don't understand that in brief. Please explain. So the Buddha goes pair by pair, as the text frames it, across lives. One who kills and is cruel tends toward a short life; one who refrains, a long one. One who harms others with fist or stick, toward sickness; one who doesn't, health. One who's quick to anger, toward a plain appearance; one who's patient, beauty. Envy, toward little influence. Not giving, toward poverty. Arrogance, refusing to honor those worthy of honor, toward low birth. And not asking the wise what's good and what's harmful, toward foolishness. Notice that last one. Wisdom, in this teaching, grows from asking questions, which is exactly what Subha is doing. In the tradition this is read as a description of how actions tend to ripen, not a ledger for judging anyone. Nothing in the discourse invites anyone to look at a sick neighbor and call them guilty. Tomorrow's discourse, the very next one, will warn against simple readings. But today's teaching has a hopeful edge. If we're heirs of our deeds, then what we do now is the inheritance we're writing. Subha, at the end, goes for refuge. The question he asked about other lives turned into a question about his own.
screen: `OWNERS AND HEIRS OF DEEDS` · `PAIR BY PAIR, ACROSS LIVES` · `WISDOM GROWS FROM ASKING` · `NOT A LEDGER FOR JUDGING` · then, large: `HEIRS OF OUR DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see one deed's fruit. Sit and settle. Think of one small thing you did a while ago, a kindness, a sharp word, a promise kept or broken, and trace what grew from it. A friendship that's easier. A silence that's still there. Don't judge yourself, just see the line from deed to fruit. Then rest with the breath, and notice: this sitting is a deed too. The bell holds the time.
Kammadayada. Heir of one's deeds: the Buddha's answer to Subha, that beings are owners and heirs of their deeds, and deeds shape how lives unfold. Today's word.
Your line: heirs of our deeds. Today, before one choice, ask what you're leaving yourself to inherit, and pick the one you'd like to receive. Day five hundred one.

howItsDone: The same words, owner and heir of one's deeds, close the five recollections of AN 5.57, which Theravada monastics and lay people recite as a daily reflection; teachers also caution against using kamma to blame people for illness or poverty.

not asking the wise what is good and harmful tends toward foolishness; asking tends toward wisdom.

fork.setup: you're Subha. the Buddha has answered your seven questions in one dense line about deeds. what do you do?
options: ask him to explain it in detail.
fork.reveal: Subha asks for the detail, and the Buddha goes through all seven pairs, one by one.

original.note: Pali kammadayada: heir of one's deeds. from the line: beings are owners and heirs of their kamma.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma means you get what you deserve, so you can judge people by their luck.
what it means: beings are heirs of their deeds, and what we do now is the inheritance we're writing.
what a scholar hears: MN 135, the Culakammavibhanga Sutta, gives seven pairs, and its opening formula about being owners and heirs of kamma also appears in the five daily recollections (AN 5.57).

MN 135 paraphrased. Confirm the seven pairs and their causes (killing, harming, anger, envy, not giving, arrogance/not honoring, not questioning).
Subha here is the same Subha Todeyyaputta of MN 99 (day 477); confirm.
